memories.content: Avoid em dashes in the proposal; split the sentence or use more ordinary punctuation instead.
The user tends to place several independently reviewable claims in one long sentence.
Use first-person active voice for choices and commitments owned by the proposal author so responsibility remains explicit throughout the work plan.
Describe prototype operations that have already been implemented and verified as observed states.
Describe prototype operations not yet implemented or evaluated as plans or expectations.
When a commitment is phrased passively, readers may interpret it as uncertainty, evasiveness, or reluctance to take responsibility.
Use “we” only for decisions and commitments the authors control, not for external facts or actions owned by another party.
The user should use one first-person pronoun consistently for the same authorial role and should not alternate between “I” and “we” unless the responsible party actually changes.
The user tends to hide unsettled commitments behind passive phrases such as “will be considered” or “is expected.”
Split proposal prose into short sentences when a sentence contains more than one independently reviewable claim.
Keep one main claim in each sentence so a reviewer can locate and assess it quickly.
The user tends to repeat em dashes when a sentence already contains several clauses.
Repeated em dashes can shift a reviewer’s attention from the proposal’s argument to suspicion that its prose was generated by AI.
Do not change names referring to the same user roles, system functions, or operational stages midway.
Use abbreviations only for long recurring terms in a two-page proposal.
Present the full term and abbreviation together when using an abbreviation for the first time.
Refer to participants based on the roles they perform in the study rather than their status.
Reviewers from different subfields find it difficult to infer an abbreviation from context alone when it is not defined at first use.
When introducing an operational role for the first time, define both the decisions it can make and the actions it performs.
Individuals holding identical job titles may possess different system modification privileges and data access rights depending on their deployment site.
The user tends to group distinct field roles under the single label “user.”

analysis.overview: Both frames promote precise, reviewable proposal prose and share a policy of stable referents. The reference frame additionally addresses sentence structure, punctuation, authorial responsibility, and prototype status, while the compared frame adds abbreviation discipline and operationally precise participant roles.

relations.reason: One claim applies consistency specifically to first-person authorial pronouns, while the other applies it to names for roles, functions, and stages; both govern stable referents without contradiction.
relations.summary: Keep references stable when the responsible party, role, function, or operational stage has not changed.

relations.reason: The memories jointly describe a recurring multi-claim sentence pattern and the corresponding proposal-writing policy for improving reviewability.
relations.summary: Use short sentences containing one independently reviewable main claim.

relations.reason: The memories state the punctuation policy, identify the recurring pattern, and explain its risk of distracting reviewers and suggesting AI-generated prose.
relations.summary: Avoid em dashes in proposal prose, especially repeated use within clause-heavy sentences.

relations.reason: The memories collectively establish an explicit-responsibility policy and explain how passive commitment language can obscure ownership or convey uncertainty and evasiveness.
relations.summary: Express author-controlled choices and commitments in first-person active voice, reserving “we” for matters the authors control.

relations.reason: The memories split one status-sensitive policy: verified implementations are observed states, whereas operations not yet implemented or evaluated are plans or expectations.
relations.summary: Match descriptions of prototype operations to their implementation and evaluation status.

relations.reason: The memories provide the selection rule, first-use convention, and reviewer-comprehension rationale for one abbreviation policy in a short proposal.
relations.summary: Use abbreviations selectively for long recurring terms and define each abbreviation with its full term at first use.

relations.reason: The memories jointly address role-based participant naming, required role definitions, site-dependent authority differences, and the tendency to collapse distinct roles into “user.”
relations.summary: Distinguish and define participants by their operational roles, decisions, actions, privileges, and access rather than generic status or job labels.

reports.both: Referents should remain consistent for unchanged roles, functions, stages, and authorial responsibility.
reports.compared_only: Abbreviations should be selective and defined at first use, while participant terminology should reflect distinct operational roles, authority, actions, and access.
reports.reference_only: Proposal prose should isolate reviewable claims, avoid repeated em dashes, state author-owned commitments actively, and distinguish observed prototype states from future plans.
